procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 05.03.2018 by the Special Judge, Bathinda, allowing an application under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, summoning the appellant (Gurdev Sigh Bhalla, Inspector) along with three other officials of the Police Department.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Gurdev Sigh Bhalla, Inspector) challenged the order of the Special Judge before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh by way of a Criminal Revision. The High Court dismissed the revision on 23rd March, 2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's order dismissing the Criminal Revision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding prima facie evidence on record to make it a triable case against the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the Revision filed by the appellant against the order of the Special Judge allowing the application u/s. 319 CrPC summoning the appellant.

facts: The appellant, a police inspector, was summoned by a Special Judge under an application filed under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
The appellant challenged this summoning order by filing a revision petition before the High Court, which was dismissed.

The appellant then appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the lower courts did not properly examine the merits of the matter, that there was no evidence to justify the summoning, and that the principles laid down in the case of Hardeep Singh vs. State of Punjab were not followed.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the case and disagreed with the appellant's contentions.
The Court found that, contrary to the appellant's claims, there was prima facie evidence on the record against the appellant.
The Court determined that this evidence was sufficient to make it a "triable case" against the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: Based on the finding of sufficient prima facie evidence to warrant a trial, the Supreme Court concluded that it was not inclined to interfere with the High Court's order. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, thereby upholding the High Court's decision to reject the appellant's revision petition.

issue.issue_text: Whether the order of the Trial Court summoning the appellant was in accordance with the principles laid down in Hardeep Singh vs. State of Punjab.

facts: The appellant challenged a summoning order issued by the Trial Court under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
The appellant argued that the order was not in accordance with the principles laid down in the case of Hardeep Singh vs. State of Punjab.
The appellant also contended that the Trial Court and High Court had not properly examined the merits of the matter to see if the ingredients required by the Hardeep Singh case were present.
law: The legal standard for summoning an additional accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. is governed by the principles and parameters established by the Constitution Bench in the case of Hardeep Singh vs. State of Punjab.
application: The Supreme Court independently reviewed the evidence that was before the Trial Court.
Specifically, the Court perused the statements recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C. and the depositions of prosecution witnesses PW-1, PW-13, and PW-18.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, finding that upon its own review of the evidence, the parameters laid down in the Hardeep Singh judgment were "fully satisfied." Therefore, the Court concluded that the Trial Court's order summoning the appellant was justified and in accordance with the law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the summoning order passed by the Trial Court was bad on merits due to a lack of evidence.

facts: The informant provided a statement with complete facts about the conduct of the police officials after his father surrendered.
The informant's statement was consistent throughout the investigation and trial.
Other witnesses, including the complainant's wife and father, gave statements with the same details.
The witnesses consistently narrated incidents involving threats, demands for a large sum of money, and the torture of the father.
law: For a summoning order under Section 319 Cr.P.C. to be valid, there must be prima facie evidence on record to make the case triable against the person being summoned.
application: The Supreme Court examined the evidence on record, particularly the statements of the informant and other witnesses.
The Court found that the consistent and detailed testimonies regarding threats, demands for money, and torture constituted sufficient evidence.
Based on these witness statements, the Court determined that there was a prima facie case against the appellant that warranted a trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that there was sufficient prima facie evidence on record to justify the Trial Court's summoning order and make it a triable case against the appellant. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the Revision filed by the appellant against the order of the Special Judge allowing the application u/s. 319 CrPC summoning the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The original complaint dated 06.09.2013 did not contain any allegations against the appellant.

The application to summon the appellant under Section 319 Cr.P.C. was a 'counter blast' filed with annoyance and vengeance because the appellant had deposed against the informant's father on the same day.
The informant's story was an attempt to brow-beat the appellant because he was the Investigating Officer in a case against the informant's father.
respondent_arguments: The lower courts (High Court and Trial Court) had correctly appreciated the evidence on record.
The appellant and other police officials had harassed and tortured not only the victim (Devraj) while in custody but also threatened and tortured his family members to extract a huge amount of money.
Statements recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C. and before the Trial Court consistently supported the allegations against the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the order of the Trial Court summoning the appellant was in accordance with the principles laid down in Hardeep Singh vs. State of Punjab.
appellant_arguments: The evidence was not strong enough to meet the high threshold for summoning under Section 319 CrPC, as suggested by the arguments that the allegations were a retaliatory 'counter blast' and an attempt to 'brow-beat' the appellant.
respondent_arguments: The evidence on record was sufficient for summoning, as demonstrated by consistent statements from multiple witnesses recorded during both the investigation and the trial, which detailed the appellant's criminal conduct.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the summoning order passed by the Trial Court was bad on merits due to a lack of evidence.
appellant_arguments: The original complaint did not name the appellant.
The story was fabricated to harass the appellant, as evidenced by the fact that the FIR mentioned only Rs. 50,000, whereas a subsequent story of Rs. 24 lakhs was set up later.
The application to summon was filed with malicious intent as a 'counter blast' to the appellant giving evidence against the informant's father.
respondent_arguments: There was sufficient prima facie evidence on record for a triable case.
The informant's statement, which provided complete facts about the police officials' conduct, was consistent throughout the investigation and trial.
The informant's statement was corroborated by other witnesses (his wife and father) who also narrated the incidents of threats, torture, and the demand for a huge sum of money.

cases.case_name: Hardeep Singh vs. State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the principles and parameters laid down for summoning an additional accused under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For a summoning order under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the parameters laid down in the Constitution Bench judgment in Hardeep Singh vs. State of Punjab must be fully satisfied based on the evidence adduced before the court.
obiter: Any observations made in an order concerning a summoning decision will not come in the way of the Trial Court in deciding the trial on its own merits based on the evidence adduced before it.
A court, when deciding on a summoning order, may refrain from a threadbare discussion of witness testimony as it may ultimately influence the Trial Court at a later stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court concluded that there is sufficient prima facie evidence on record to establish a triable case against the appellant, thereby justifying the summoning order issued by the Trial Court under Section 319 Cr.P.C. and the High Court's dismissal of the revision petition.
legal_tests_applied: The standard for summoning an accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. is whether there is prima facie evidence on record to make it a triable case against the person being summoned.
why_appellant_lost: The Court found the appellant's primary argument—that the allegations were fabricated to 'brow-beat' him in retaliation for giving evidence against the informant's father—to be 'difficult to accept'.
The Court determined that, contrary to the appellant's claim of a lack of evidence, there was sufficient 'prima facie evidence on record to make it a triable case as against the appellant.'
why_respondent_won: The Court's finding affirmed the respondent's position that there was sufficient evidence for the trial to proceed, stating 'there appears to be prima facie evidence on record to make it a triable case as against the appellant.'
policy_considerations: The Court deliberately avoided a detailed discussion of witness testimony to prevent influencing the lower court, stating, 'we are not threadbare discussing the testimony of the witness during the trial as it may ultimately influence the Trial Court at a later stage.'

To ensure a fair trial, the Court explicitly directed that its observations should not prejudice the Trial Court's independent assessment of the evidence, clarifying that 'any observations made in this order will not come in the way of the Trial Court in deciding the trial on its own merits... completely uninfluenced by this judgment.'
